Dashed frame: region watched. Thin lines: grid of latitude and longitude.

▲ Station shown in the waveform panel. △ Other station watched: click it to show its record. A station outside the map (NIL) is drawn at the edge with its distance.

◯ Ring around a station: it is shaking now, larger when stronger. Black: ordinary signal. Red: a warning or alarm of a potential landslide / avalanche applies to it.

Grey band or area: where the source of the newest signal can lie, worked out from its arrival times at two or three stations. Darker: glaciers near.

Place names appear when the map is zoomed in: states and cities first, then the districts and municipalities of Nepal.

Temperature: air temperature 2 m above ground from the Open-Meteo weather model at 153 points, asked about once an hour. Between the points it is worked out from the terrain height (6.5 °C per km, cells of about 5 km): an estimate, not a measurement. While it is shown, borders, rivers and glaciers are drawn in black and white.

Alarm rules

Four stations are watched: NK.KKN, IO.EVN, IN.SHL and II.NIL (open and sending when checked on 13 Nov 2026). II.NIL (Nilore, Pakistan) lies about 440 km north-west of the mapped area and is drawn at the edge of the map; it is the only open live station towards Himachal and Kashmir, and the pairing rules of the network check were not tested with it. The waveform panel and the alarm rules use one station at a time: the one that recorded the newest signal first, or the one picked on the map. While live the other stations come over the same live stream and their records are searched every 15 seconds; if the stream does not deliver, the archive service is read every 3 minutes instead, and their signals and rings can then be several minutes behind. The limits below were set for NK.KKN and are untested at the other stations.

Network check: every warning and alarm names the other stations that recorded a signal at the same time (at least 20 s long and 6 times the background, no further from the first onset than the first waves need between the two stations plus 10 s, and the station reached first not more than 5 times weaker). It does not change the level. When two or more stations recorded it clearly (10 times the background), the map shows in grey where the source can lie: a band for two stations, an area for three. Tested on 13 Nov 2026 with listed earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 to 5.6 from 2024 to 2026 (USGS): the band of NK.KKN and IO.EVN held the listed epicentre for 22 of 23 events, among them the 26 Aug 2026 collapse, and covered 35% of the region watched (median; 2% to 40%), so it narrows the search but does not give a place. All three stations recorded two earthquakes clearly: the areas were about 14,000 and 78,000 km² and the listed epicentres lay 11 and 7 km outside them. With IN.SHL as one of only two stations (two earthquakes) the band missed the epicentre by 12 and by 135 km. An unrelated signal at IO.EVN falls into the window of a signal at NK.KKN in fewer than 2 of 100 cases (estimated from the signal rates in 10 to 19 hours of ordinary record). The wave speeds were fitted to the same earthquakes, so this is not an independent test. IN.SHL did not record the 26 Aug 2026 collapse, so that source gives a band, not an area.

Notice: a new event appears in the lists. Warning sign: a long, low-frequency signal reaches the station before any list entry, or a listed event does not look like an ordinary earthquake. Alarm: a listed event in glacier terrain shows at least two of the signs below (potential landslide / avalanche), or the shaking has not stopped half an hour after it began (potential debris flow / flood).

Rings on the map: a station gets a ring when its last 10 seconds are at least 3 times its usual level (the middle value of the last hour); the ring grows by a fixed step for every tenfold increase. Red: a warning or alarm that has not been explained as an ordinary earthquake belongs to that signal. Black: any other signal.

Signs: the shaking builds up slowly; it is very slow (much of its energy below 0.2 Hz); it lasts much longer than usual for the magnitude and distance; it does not fade, or grows again. The limits were set on 11 Nov 2026 from the public record of station NK.KKN (Kakani, Nepal): the Rasuwa collapse of 26 Aug 2026 and six earthquakes of magnitude 4.3 to 5.6 at 200 to 440 km. Seven events are a small sample, and other stations may need other limits.

Connection log

About

Prototype for a class project. It is not a warning system and must not be used as one. Alarms from a past record are labelled REPLAY.

Event lists: EMSC SeismicPortal (CC BY 4.0) and USGS Earthquake Hazards Program. Waveforms: EarthScope and GEOFON (GFZ) data services and the operators of the station shown. Glaciers: Randolph Glacier Inventory 7.0, regions 13 to 15, outlines dated 1989 to 2010, simplified to about 80 m; the alarm rule uses the same inventory reduced to 0.05° cells. Rivers: derived from the terrain model of the project (basins over 400 km²); in flat land the lines can lie beside the real channel. Borders: COD-AB (Nepal) and Natural Earth 10m (other countries), as drawn in the sources; disputed sections are not marked. Contour lines every 500 m (below 500 m also at 50 to 400 m, shown when zoomed in): from Copernicus DEM GLO-90 resampled to 250 m, simplified to about 200 m and drawn as smooth curves when zoomed in; closed lines shorter than 3.5 km are left out. Around Rasuwa (about 85.0 to 85.8°E, 27.8 to 28.6°N) the lines come from the project's 30 m model (Copernicus DEM GLO-30) once the map is zoomed in, every 100 m further in; at the edge of that area they do not meet the regional lines exactly. Place names: Natural Earth 10m populated places and state labels (public domain) and COD-AB Nepal (provinces, districts, municipalities), spelled as in the sources. Temperature layer: weather data by Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0), air temperature 2 m above ground at 153 points; between the points it is an estimate from the terrain height (Copernicus DEM GLO-90 in 0.05° cells, 6.5 °C per km), not a measurement; in a strip along the southern edge (south of about 25.1°N), where that terrain model ends, the height is taken from ETOPO1 (10 arc-minutes). Waveform reading: seisplotjs 3.2.7 (MIT). Times are UTC; Nepal time is UTC + 5:45. Waveform panel: top, ground motion with signals shaded and the expected first waves of listed events dashed; bottom, frequency from 0 to 10 Hz with the limit for very slow shaking in red.
